title: Fat-Tree QRAM: A High-Bandwidth Shared Quantum Random Access Memory for Parallel Queries
problem: Existing Quantum Random Access Memory (QRAM) architectures, particularly Bucket-Brigade (BB) QRAM, cannot process multiple queries in parallel because the binary tree root node is exclusively occupied for the entire duration of each query, forcing all queries to queue and execute sequentially. In a shared memory system with multiple QPUs, this causes total query latency to scale as O(p*log(N)) for p parallel processes, bottlenecking parallel quantum algorithms.
motivation: Parallel quantum algorithms (distributed Shor's, parallel QSP, Hamiltonian simulation, k-Sum) critically depend on high-bandwidth QRAM capable of simultaneous queries; the sequential nature of BB QRAM fundamentally limits quantum computing throughput in shared memory systems.
method: Fat-Tree QRAM replaces single router nodes with multiple router copies in a tree structure: the root contains log(N) copies while the leaves contain one (matching the traditional design). This allows different queries to flow through different routers simultaneously instead of all queueing at a single control point. Each query progresses through alternating steps: addressing steps that load the target memory address using CSWAP gates (quantum operations that conditionally swap values between qubits, taking 4 circuit layers), and routing steps using local SWAP gates within each router node (taking 1 circuit layer per step). Two alternating SWAP types—SWAP-I and SWAP-II—cycle each query through progressively larger QRAM sub-components while keeping all data movement local within individual nodes.
key_novelty: Fat-Tree QRAM achieves parallel quantum memory access by duplicating the bottleneck control node throughout the tree (log(N) copies at the root instead of one), enabling O(log(N)) queries to pipeline simultaneously while using O(N) qubits and maintaining constant access speed independent of memory size.
contributions: Fat-Tree QRAM architecture pipelining O(log(N)) independent queries in O(log(N)) time with O(N) qubits — constant factor qubit overhead vs. BB QRAM
Modular (coaxial-cable-linked) and on-chip (bi-planar, TSV-connected) hardware implementations for superconducting circuits with bi-planar nearest-neighbor connectivity sufficiency proof
FIFO query scheduling protocol proven optimal for minimizing total query latency; analysis of hardware utilization and QRAM bandwidth metrics
Demonstrated circuit depth reduction of up to 10x for parallel quantum algorithms (Grover's, k-Sum, Hamiltonian simulation, QSP) at N=2^10 vs. BB and Virtual QRAM baselines

metrics.speedup: up to 10x circuit depth reduction for parallel quantum algorithms vs. BB and Virtual QRAM at N=2^10
metrics.area: 16N qubits (vs. 8N for BB QRAM) — 2x qubit overhead for log(N)-fold parallelism
metrics.accuracy: same infidelity scaling as BB QRAM: O(log^2(N)*epsilon) per query
metrics.other: constant QRAM bandwidth (independent of N) vs. O(1/log(N)) for BB QRAM; amortized single-query latency 8.25 circuit layers (constant) vs. 8*log(N) for BB

limitations: Fat-Tree QRAM requires rapid classical memory swapping with constant time intervals between queries, which may be challenging in practice for large classical memory; the paper notes this as an open hardware challenge.
primary_theme: high-bandwidth parallel-query quantum random access memory
